opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started with a pretty simple kind of admiration. I was in middle school when I first played Rainblood. It was a small, dark, very stylish wuxia RPG, and what struck me wasn't only the gameplay. It was the mood, the writing, the sense that one person had a very particular aesthetic vision and pushed it all the way through. It didn't feel like a commercial product made by committee. It felt like an author's work.

Then I learned a bit about the person behind it, and that was the moment it clicked for me. This wasn't some giant studio. It was basically a young person, a student, making something on their own with tools like RPG Maker, and it reached so many players. As a kid in a fairly ordinary environment, I realized that making games was something real people did, people not that different from me.

I also noticed that a lot of the people I looked up to then, the ones doing interesting things in games, tech, or the internet, had gone through top universities. I'm not saying that's the only path, and looking back it's a little naive. But at the time, getting into a really good school felt like the entrance to that world. It was where you'd meet people who thought the same way, where you'd have the freedom and resources to try building things.

So my motivation to study hard wasn't really about prestige in the abstract. It was more like, "If I want to someday make something that moves people the way Rainblood moved me, I need to get myself into the place where that's possible." That gave me a very concrete reason to grind through all the exam pressure. The game was the spark, and school was the road I thought would take me there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I was fourteen when I first played Rainblood. It was this little indie wuxia RPG, made almost entirely by one person, Liang Qiwei, in RPG Maker. What struck me wasn't the graphics or the mechanics, honestly. It was the realization that one person, sitting alone somewhere, could build an entire world with its own atmosphere, its own morality, its own way of talking. Before that, I thought games came from faceless companies. Rainblood made creation feel personal and possible.

And that raised a question for me that I couldn't shake: how do you become the kind of person who can do that? I started reading about Liang's background, about where other indie creators came from, and I noticed a pattern. A lot of them had been exposed, often through university, to people and ideas that pushed them beyond what their hometown or their high school offered. Not because elite schools teach you how to make games. They mostly don't. But because they put you in a room with people who take ambitious, strange projects seriously.

So for me the drive to get into a top university wasn't really about prestige or a safe career path. It was about access to that density of serious, curious people. I wanted to be around others who would look at a weird idea and ask "how do we build it" rather than "why bother." Rainblood gave me the hunger to make things. The university was supposed to be where I'd find the people and the tools to actually do it.

In hindsight, that's a slightly romantic view of elite education. The reality was messier. But the romantic version is what got me through the exam years, so I'm grateful to that game for it.
